content.text: Energy is one of the most fundamental concepts in all of science. It governs everything from the motion of planets to the chemical reactions in your body. Yet energy itself is surprisingly hard to define — it is not a substance you can hold or see. Instead, energy is best understood as a quantity that is conserved: it can be transferred from one store to another, but it can never be created or destroyed.

In this lesson, we will explore the different ways energy can be stored, the mechanisms by which it is transferred, and the all-important law of conservation of energy. We will also learn the mathematical expressions for kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy, and develop skills in using energy transfer diagrams and Sankey diagrams.

Energy is transferred between stores through several mechanisms (or pathways):
When a force moves an object, energy is transferred by

(or simply "work"). For example, pushing a box across a floor transfers energy from your chemical store to the kinetic energy store of the box (and to the thermal energy store of the box and floor through friction).
When a current flows through a circuit, energy is transferred by
. For example, a battery (chemical store) transfers energy through an electrical pathway to a bulb (which transfers energy to light and thermal stores).
Energy is transferred from a hotter region to a cooler region by
. This can occur through conduction, convection, or radiation. For example, a hot cup of coffee transfers energy to the surrounding air by heating.
(radiation). The Sun transfers energy to the Earth by radiation. A light bulb transfers energy to its surroundings by radiation (light and infrared).
Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one store to another or transformed from one form to another. The total energy of a closed system remains constant.
This is one of the most fundamental laws in physics. It applies universally — there are no known exceptions.

In practice, when energy is transferred, some energy is almost always transferred to thermal energy stores (through friction, air resistance, or electrical resistance). This energy is often described as "wasted" or "dissipated," but it has not been destroyed — it has simply been spread out into the surroundings in a way that is not useful.

are a special type of energy transfer diagram where the width of the arrows is proportional to the amount of energy. They clearly show:
The total energy input (wide arrow entering from the left)
The useful energy output (arrow continuing to the right)
The wasted energy (arrows branching off, usually downward)
The total width of all output arrows must equal the width of the input arrow (conservation of energy).

For example, a light bulb with 100 J of electrical energy input might produce 10 J of light energy and 90 J of thermal energy. The Sankey diagram would show a wide input arrow splitting into a thin arrow (light, 10% of width) and a thick arrow (thermal, 90% of width).

Energy is never used up. It is transferred or transformed. When we say a battery is "used up," we mean the chemical energy has been transferred to other stores. The total energy in the universe remains constant.
Energy cannot be created. Power stations do not create energy — they transfer energy from one store (e.g., chemical energy in fuel or nuclear energy) to another (electrical energy).
"Kinetic energy depends on velocity, just like momentum."
. Doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy but only doubles the momentum.
"GPE depends on the total height of the object."
GPE depends on the height above a chosen reference level. The change in GPE is what matters physically, and it depends on the change in height, not the absolute height.
"Heat and thermal energy are the same."

"Thermal energy" is the energy stored in the random motion of particles within an object. "Heating" (or "heat") is the process of transferring energy from a hotter object to a cooler one. Heat is a transfer mechanism, not a store.
Wasted energy is not destroyed — it is dissipated (spread out) into the surroundings, usually as thermal energy. It still exists but is no longer in a useful, concentrated form.
